definition: Verdant means green with growing plants.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word verdant. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know verdant should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Rice terraces climb the hillside in verdant steps that glow against the grey stone above them.
Grassy states a bare fact — grass grows here, thick or thin; it claims less than verdant, which wants living green in real quantity.
Lush goes past verdant — beyond green and into extravagance, growth so thick it crowds and spills over itself.

Green is the plain everyday word, and it is only a color — a painted door and a spring hillside earn it equally. Verdant claims more: green with growing plants, chlorophyll actually at work, a green that no paint can fake.

Leafy is green specifically with foliage — trees and shrubs, branches overhead, leaves you could gather by the armful. Verdant asks only for growth: a cropped pasture or a barley plot is verdant with not a tree in sight.

From the last dune crest the caravan saw it a full hour before reaching it: a verdant smudge floating on the shimmer, date palms over barley plots over channels of led water.
The drivers, who had watched rock and gravel for nine days, said nothing.
The youngest rider counted shades on the way in and gave up at six kinds of green.
Verdant is the exact word for that oasis, because it means green with growing plants — living green, green that is busy photosynthesizing, not painted on.
The word does not require trees, lushness, or rain; it requires growth.
Wherever chlorophyll is at work in quantity, from barley plots to a well-kept lawn, verdant applies.
Verdant is green upgraded for the page — travel writing, brochures, poems about spring.
It claims living green and nothing more: for growth so thick it overwhelms, step up to lush, and when the green world you mean is specifically woods, this unit's sylvan carries the forest with it.
A cropped pasture can be perfectly verdant; nobody would call it lush.

The volunteers who replanted the old quarry did not expect much the first year.
Crushed rock holds little water, and the seed mix they scattered was cheap — clover, vetch, and a hardy prairie rye.

The pit that had been gray rubble for forty years had turned verdant from rim to floor, so thickly covered that the rock never showed through.
A botanist who surveyed it counted forty species and wrote, with evident pleasure, that the quarry was now the liveliest patch of ground in the county.
